l: river Oeroe, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER IV.
s: The river Oeroe lies on the route from Platæa to Thebes. It is said to have been the daughter of Asopus.

l: Asopus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER IV.
s: The Asopus lies near the river Oeroe and is still the boundary between the districts of Platæa and Thebes.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER V.
s: The unit recounts the early history of Thebes, from the Ectenes, Hyantes, and Aones through the arrival of Cadmus and the establishment of Cadmea. It traces the Theban royal line through Cadmus, Laius, Oedipus, Polynices, and Eteocles, including the conflicts that led to changes in the city’s rulers. It also discusses Amphion’s musical fame, Oedipus’s patricide and incest, and the later wars between Thebes and Argos.

l: Thebes, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER V.
s: Thebes was first said to have been inhabited by the Ectenes under King Ogygus, then repeopled by the Hyantes and Aones. Cadmus built Cadmea, which later became the citadel of lower Thebes, and Amphion and Zethus joined the lower town to Cadmea and named it Thebes after Thebe. The city later endured dynastic conflicts, Argive invasions, and the migration of some of its rulers.

l: Cadmus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER V.
s: Cadmus invaded the land with a Phoenician army, defeated the Hyantes, and allowed the submissive Aones to remain and mix with the Phoenicians. He built Cadmea and chose Echion as his son-in-law because of Echion’s valour. Cadmus later migrated to the Illyrians called Enchelians and was succeeded by his son Polydorus.

l: Cadmea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER V.
s: Cadmea was the town built by Cadmus. As the settlement grew, it became the citadel of lower Thebes, and Amphion and Zethus later joined the lower town to it.

l: Laius, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER V.
s: Laius was the son of Labdacus and was entrusted to Lycus after Labdacus died. He was restored to the kingdom after the family of Amphion and Zethus was destroyed, but the oracle at Delphi warned that a son born to him by Jocasta would kill him. Laius therefore exposed Oedipus, though Oedipus eventually killed him.

l: Amphion, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER V.
s: Amphion and his brother Zethus invaded Thebes and defeated Lycus, while those loyal to Cadmus’s line withdrew Laius. Amphion and Zethus joined the lower town to Cadmea and named it Thebes after Thebe. Amphion was famous for music, was said to have expanded the lyre from four strings to seven, and was later punished in Hades for railing against Leto and her sons.

l: Euryganea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER V.
s: Euryganea, the daughter of Hyperphas, was said to be the mother of Oedipus’s four children rather than Jocasta. The painter Onatas depicted her dejected by the quarrels of her sons.

l: Œdipus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER V.
s: Oedipus was exposed by Laius because of the Delphic oracle but was fated to grow up, kill his father, and marry his mother. Pausanias argues from Homer that Oedipus had no children by Jocasta and that his children were by Euryganea. During Oedipus’s lifetime, Polynices left Thebes fearing that his father’s curses would be fulfilled, and Oedipus’s death preceded Polynices’ return.

l: Jocasta, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER V.
s: Jocasta married Laius, whose oracle warned that a son born to her would kill him. Oedipus later married her after killing Laius, though Pausanias maintains that they had no children together.

l: Polynices, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER V.
s: Polynices left Thebes during Oedipus’s lifetime because he feared that his father’s curses would be fulfilled. He went to Argos, married the daughter of Adrastus, and returned after Oedipus’s death when Eteocles sent for him. After quarrelling with Eteocles and going into exile again, he obtained an army from Adrastus, fought Eteocles in single combat, and died with him; his son Thersander later inherited the Theban line.

l: Eteocles, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER V.
s: Eteocles sent for Polynices after Oedipus’s death, but the brothers quarrelled when Polynices returned. Eteocles and Polynices challenged each other and killed one another, after which the kingdom passed to Laodamas, Eteocles’s son.

l: Oedipus's patricide and incest, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER V.
s: Oedipus was fated to kill his father, Laius, and to marry his mother, Jocasta, after doing so. Homer says that the gods soon made the relationship publicly known; Pausanias uses this to argue that Oedipus and Jocasta did not have children together.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VI.
s: The Thebans were defeated twice by the Athenians but later defeated them at Delium. They were first friendly with the Lacedæmonians after the Persian departure, then joined the Corinthians against them and achieved a major victory at the battle of Leuctra. The Thebans later fought for ten years in the Sacred War and suffered especially heavily in the Greek defeat at the battle of Chæronea, after which a Macedonian garrison was placed in Thebes. Following Philip's death, the Thebans expelled the garrison, despite omens warning of their coming ruin.

l: Thebans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VI.
s: The Thebans were defeated by the Athenians in two battles, including one near Platæa, but later defeated the Athenians at Delium. They were first friendly with the Lacedæmonians, then joined the Corinthians against them, and won the battle of Leuctra, after which they removed Lacedæmonian decemvirates and Harmosts from the towns. They fought for ten years in the Sacred War, suffered especially heavily at Chæronea, and later expelled the Macedonian garrison from Thebes after Philip's death.

l: Thebes, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VI.
s: Thebes was ruled by an oligarchy when its forces appeared to favor king Xerxes over Greece. After the defeat at Chæronea, a Macedonian garrison was placed in Thebes; after Philip's death and Alexander's accession, the garrison was expelled, and omens at the temple of Demeter Thesmophorus warned of Thebes' ruin.

l: Athenians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VI.
s: The Athenians defeated the Thebans while fighting on the side of the Platæans in a border war and defeated them again near Platæa. They were later defeated by the Thebans at Delium, where their general Hippocrates, son of Ariphron, died with most of his army.

l: Lacedæmonians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VI.
s: The Lacedæmonians were initially friendly with the Thebans after the departure of the Medes. After the war between the Peloponnesians and the Athenians, the Thebans joined the Corinthians against them; the Lacedæmonians defeated the Thebans at Corinth and Coronea but were defeated at Leuctra, after which their decemvirates and Harmosts were removed from their towns.

l: battle of Leuctra, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VI.
s: The battle of Leuctra was a famous victory by the Thebans over the Lacedæmonians and is described as the most famous of the known battles between Greeks. After it, the Thebans put down the decemvirates established by the Lacedæmonians and expelled their Harmosts.

l: battle of Chæronea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VI.
s: The battle of Chæronea is described as a reverse that befell all the Greeks, falling most heavily on the Thebans. A Macedonian garrison was subsequently placed in Thebes.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VII.
s: The Thebans were expelled from Thebes by Alexander, fled to Athens, and were restored by Cassander the son of Antipater with help from the Athenians, Messenians, and Arcadians of Megalopolis. Cassander opposed Alexander's family, but his sons later suffered violent deaths and his house was punished. The Thebans rebuilt their walls, then joined Mithridates in war against Rome, repented when Sulla invaded Bœotia, and lost half of Thebais before later recovering it through Roman favor. In the narrator's time, the lower part of Thebes was deserted except for its temples, while the citadel remained inhabited.

l: Thebans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VII.
s: The Thebans were expelled from Thebes by Alexander, escaped to Athens, and were restored by Cassander the son of Antipater with assistance from the Athenians, Messenians, and Arcadians of Megalopolis. They rebuilt their old walls, later joined Mithridates in his war against Rome, and sought renewed Roman friendship after Sulla invaded Bœotia. Sulla took half their territory, though they later recovered it through Roman favor; in the narrator's time, the lower part of their city was largely deserted.

l: Thebes, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VII.
s: Thebes was the city from which the Thebans were expelled by Alexander and to which they were restored by Cassander. Its old walls were rebuilt, but the city later became progressively weaker; in the narrator's time, only its temples and the inhabited citadel remained, with the citadel called Thebes rather than Cadmea.

l: Alexander, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VII.
s: Alexander expelled the Thebans from Thebes. Cassander restored Thebes chiefly out of hatred for Alexander and sought to destroy Alexander's house.

l: Cassander, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VII.
s: Cassander restored the Thebans to Thebes, chiefly because of his hatred for Alexander. He ordered the Macedonians to stone Olympias, Alexander's mother, and poisoned Alexander's sons, Hercules and Alexander. Cassander died suffering from dropsy and worms, and his sons later met violent or untimely ends.

l: Athenians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VII.
s: The Athenians were very friendly in the restoration of Thebes and helped the Thebans return. The Thebans later joined Mithridates in his war against Rome, apparently out of friendship for the Athenian people.

l: Athens, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VII.
s: Athens received the Thebans after Alexander expelled them from Thebes.

l: Mithridates, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VII.
s: Mithridates was opposed to Rome in a war that the Thebans joined, apparently because of their friendship with the Athenian people.

l: Sulla, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VII.
s: Sulla invaded Bœotia during the war with Mithridates, causing panic among the Thebans when they repented of their alliance and sought renewed friendship with Rome. He remained angry with them, took half their territory, and gave the gods half of Thebais in exchange for the votive offerings he had distributed to his troops.

l: Thebais, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VII.
s: Sulla took half of Thebais from the Thebans, giving it to the gods in return for votive offerings collected from Olympia, Epidaurus, and Delphi. The Thebans later recovered the land through the favor of the Romans.

l: war with Mithridates, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VII.
s: The Thebans joined Mithridates in his war against Rome, apparently out of friendship for the Athenian people. Sulla's invasion of Bœotia during this war caused the Thebans to panic and seek renewed friendship with Rome.

l: restoration of Thebes, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VII.
s: The restoration of Thebes followed the expulsion of the Thebans by Alexander. Cassander carried it out with assistance from the Athenians, Messenians, and Arcadians of Megalopolis.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VIII.
s: The text describes the ruins of Potniæ, its grove, local rites, the temple of Dionysus Ægobolus, and traditions about a well that makes horses mad. It then identifies the supposed place where Amphiaraus was swallowed by the earth. At Thebes, seven gates remain within the old walls, each with a name and an associated explanation. The account also describes the Thebans' flight to Homole and return through the gate Homolois, and says that Capaneus was struck by lightning at Electris.

l: Thebes, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VIII.
s: Thebes had seven gates within the circuit of its old walls, and all of them retained their names. The road from Potniæ led back to Thebes, and the road from Platæa entered it through Electris.

l: Potniæ, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VIII.
s: Potniæ was a ruined place about 10 stades from Thebes, with a grove dedicated to Demeter and Proserpine and statues by the river called the Potnian goddesses. Its people performed rites involving sucking pigs, maintained a temple of Dionysus Ægobolus, and showed a well believed to make local horses mad if they drank from it.

l: Dionysus Ægobolus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VIII.
s: Dionysus Ægobolus, or Goat-killer, had a temple at Potniæ. After the people killed his priest while drunk, a pestilence came upon them, and Delphi instructed them to sacrifice a grown boy; not many years later, the god is said to have accepted a goat instead.

l: Amphiaraus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VIII.
s: Amphiaraus was believed to have been swallowed by the earth in a small enclosure marked by pillars on the road between Potniæ and Thebes. It was said that neither birds sat on the pillars nor tame or wild animals fed on the grass there.

l: seven gates of Thebes, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VIII.
s: The seven gates within the old walls of Thebes were Electris, Prœtisis, Neiste, Crenæa, Highest, Ogygia, and Homolois. The text gives explanations or traditions for the names of each gate.

l: Electris, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VIII.
s: Electris was named after Electra, the sister of Cadmus. The road from Platæa entered Thebes through this gate, and it was said to be the place where Capaneus was struck by lightning while attacking the walls.

l: Homolois, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VIII.
s: Homolois was the most recently named of the seven gates, while Ogygia was considered the oldest-named. It was named in memory of Homole because the Thebans who returned with Thersander entered Thebes through it.

l: Homole, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VIII.
s: Homole was described as the most fertile and well-watered of the Thessalian mountains. The Thebans who had fled after being defeated by the Argives occupied it before Thersander restored them to Thebes.

l: Thebans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VIII.
s: After being defeated in battle by the Argives at Glisas, most of the Thebans fled with Laodamas, while others avoided going to the Illyrii and settled in Homole. Thersander later restored them to Thebes, and they commemorated Homole by naming a gate Homolois.

l: Capaneus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VIII.
s: Capaneus, the son of Hipponous, made a violent attack on the walls of Thebes at Electris. He was said to have been struck by lightning there.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER IX.
s: The Argives fought the Thebans in a major war that began with a battle at Ismenius, where the Thebans were initially defeated but later destroyed the Peloponnesian army except for Adrastus. The Thebans suffered heavy losses, giving rise to the expression "Cadmean victory." Later, the Epigoni, led by Thersander, marched against Thebes with forces from several regions and defeated the Thebans at Glisas, after which some fled with Laodamas and the rest were subdued by blockade. The epic poem called the Thebais concerns this later war, which was fought over the sons of Œdipus.

l: war between the Argives and the Thebans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER IX.
s: The war was fought between the Argives and the Thebans over the sons of Œdipus. The Argive army came from the middle of the Peloponnese to the middle of Bœotia, and the conflict included the battles at Ismenius and Glisas.

l: Argives, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER IX.
s: The Argives brought an army from the middle of the Peloponnese into Bœotia and were joined by allies from Arcadia and Messenia. They defeated the Thebans at the first onset at Ismenius but were later destroyed, except for Adrastus.

l: Thebans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER IX.
s: The Thebans were initially beaten at Ismenius but defended themselves from the walls of Thebes and then destroyed the remaining Peloponnesian army. They later fought the Epigoni at Glisas, were defeated, and were either driven into flight or reduced after a blockade.

l: Peloponnese, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER IX.
s: The Argive host came from the middle of the Peloponnese to the middle of Bœotia. Peloponnesian forces were destroyed at Ismenius except for Adrastus.

l: Bœotia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER IX.
s: Bœotia was the region to which the Argive host came from the middle of the Peloponnese. The battle at Ismenius took place there.

l: Adrastus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER IX.
s: Adrastus gathered allies from Arcadia and Messenia for the Argive side. He was the only survivor of the army destroyed by the Thebans at Ismenius.

l: battle of Ismenius, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER IX.
s: At the battle of Ismenius, the Thebans were defeated at the first onset and fled to Thebes. They then killed many attackers from the walls, sallied against the army, and destroyed it except for Adrastus, though they also suffered heavy losses.

l: Ismenius, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER IX.
s: Ismenius was the place where the Argives and Thebans fought the battle in which the Thebans ultimately destroyed the Peloponnesian army.

l: Thebes, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER IX.
s: After being routed at Ismenius, the Thebans fled to Thebes and defended the city from its walls. The Epigoni later marched against Thebes and defeated its defenders at Glisas before reducing the remaining Thebans by blockade.

l: Cadmean victory, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER IX.
s: A victory won with heavy losses to the victors was called a Cadmean victory by the Thebans after their costly victory at Ismenius.

l: Epigoni, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER IX.
s: The Epigoni marched against Thebes not many years after the war involving Adrastus. Their army included forces from Argolis, Messenia, Arcadia, Corinth, and Megara, and they defeated the Thebans at Glisas.

l: Thersander, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER IX.
s: Thersander led the Epigoni in their march against Thebes.

l: battle of Glisas, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER IX.
s: The battle of Glisas was a sharp and well-contested fight between the Epigoni and the Thebans. The Thebans were defeated; some fled with Laodamas, while the rest were reduced after a blockade.

l: Glisas, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER IX.
s: Glisas was the place where the Epigoni and the Thebans fought their later battle. The Thebans were defeated there.

l: Thebais, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER IX.
s: The epic poem called the Thebais concerns the war of the Epigoni against Thebes. Callinus said that Homer wrote it, but the text considers it later than the Iliad and Odyssey.

l: sons of Œdipus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER IX.
s: The war between the Argives and the Thebans was fought over the sons of Œdipus.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER X.
s: Near the gates of Thebes are a sepulchre for those who fell fighting Alexander and the Macedonians, and a place associated with Cadmus sowing the dragon’s teeth. The hill sacred to Apollo, the god, and the river beside it are all called Ismenius, and the Temple of Ismenian Apollo contains statues and offerings, including a cedarwood statue of Apollo by Canachus. The Thebans annually choose a well-born, handsome, and strong youth as priest of Ismenian Apollo, who wears a laurel crown and may dedicate a bronze tripod. Above the temple is a spring sacred to Ares and the tomb of Caanthus, whom Apollo killed after Caanthus set fire to the grove while seeking his sister Melia.

l: Thebes, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER X.
s: Thebes has a sepulchre near its gates for those who fell in battle against Alexander and the Macedonians. Its people say that Cadmus sowed the dragon’s teeth near the gates, and they annually choose a well-born, handsome, and strong youth as priest to Ismenian Apollo.

l: Cadmus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER X.
s: Cadmus is said to have slain a dragon by a well and sown its teeth in the ground near the gates of Thebes. The ground supposedly produced a crop of armed men from the teeth.

l: hill sacred to Apollo, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER X.
s: A hill sacred to Apollo stands on the right of the gates. The hill, Apollo, and the river flowing by it are all called Ismenius.

l: Apollo, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER X.
s: Apollo is worshipped at the hill and Temple of Ismenian Apollo, where his statue resembles the one at Branchidae and is attributed to Canachus; the Ismenian statue is made of cedarwood. He is said to have given Tenerus the power of divination, named the river Ismenius after Ismenius, and killed Caanthus with an arrow after Caanthus set fire to his grove.

l: Ismenius River, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER X.
s: The river flowing by the hill sacred to Apollo is called Ismenius, as are the hill and the god. It may previously have been called Ladon before the birth of Apollo’s son Ismenius.

l: Temple of Ismenian Apollo, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER X.
s: The Temple of Ismenian Apollo has stone statues of Athene and Hermes at its entrance, called gods of the Vestibule; the Hermes is by Phidias and the Athene by Scopas. Inside is a cedarwood statue of Apollo attributed to Canachus, and nearby is Manto’s seat, the stone where Manto is said to have sat, along with statues of Henioche and Pyrrha.

l: spring sacred to Ares, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER X.
s: A spring said to be sacred to Ares lies somewhat higher than the Temple of Apollo Ismenius. Ares is said to have placed a dragon there to guard it.

l: Caanthus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER X.
s: Caanthus is said to have been the brother of Melia and the son of Oceanus. Sent by his father to find Melia after she was carried off, he found her with Apollo, set fire to the grove of Ismenian Apollo, and was killed by Apollo with an arrow; his tomb is near the spring sacred to Ares.

l: Melia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER X.
s: Melia is said to have been the daughter of Oceanus and the sister of Caanthus. Apollo had carried her off, and Caanthus found her with Apollo while searching for her.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XI.
s: The Thebans identify ruins near the Electris gate as the house where Amphitryon lived after fleeing Tiryns, and they show Alcmena’s bridal-bed and the monument of Hercules’ sons by Megara. They say that Hercules, in madness, tried to kill Amphitryon but was stopped when Athene caused a stone called Composer to strike him. The unit describes the temple of Hercules called Champion, its statues, and the story of Daedalus and Icarus. It also mentions the 12 Labours of Hercules carved by Praxiteles and an altar of Apollo Spodius near a gymnasium and racecourse dedicated to Hercules.

l: Amphitryon, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XI.
s: Amphitryon is said to have lived in the house whose ruins stand left of the Electris gate after fleeing Tiryns because of the death of Electryon. The Thebans say that Hercules, in madness, wished to kill him, but sleep overcame Hercules after Athene threw the stone called Composer.

l: bridal-bed of Alcmena, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XI.
s: The bridal-bed of Alcmena is shown among the ruins of Amphitryon’s house. It was made for Amphitryon by Trophonius and Agamedes, according to an inscription.

l: Alcmena, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XI.
s: Alcmena is associated with the bridal-bed in Amphitryon’s ruined house. The Thebans say that Hera sent the Sorceresses to prevent her childbirth, but Historis deceived them, after which Alcmena gave birth to a boy.

l: Hercules, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XI.
s: The Thebans show the monument of Hercules’ sons by Megara and say that Hercules, in madness, also wished to kill Amphitryon. He is honored in a temple called Champion, near a gymnasium and racecourse named after him, and colossal statues of Hercules and Athene were offered there by Thrasybulus and the Athenians.

l: temple of Hercules called Champion, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XI.
s: The temple of Hercules called Champion contains a white-stone statue of Hercules by Xenocritus and Eubius, both Thebans, as well as an old wooden statue believed to be by Daedalus. Colossal statues of Athene and Hercules in Pentelican marble were also offered to this temple.

l: Dædalus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XI.
s: Daedalus is believed to have made the old wooden statue of Hercules in the temple called Champion. He fled from Crete in boats he made for himself and Icarus, using sails to gain an advantage over the rowed boats of Minos.

l: Icarus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XI.
s: Icarus, the son of Daedalus, steered his boat awkwardly, causing it to overturn, and was drowned. Hercules found and recognized his body and buried it by a promontory jutting into the Aegean Sea; the island and nearby sea were then named after Icarus.

l: 12 Labours of Hercules, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XI.
s: Praxiteles carved most of the 12 Labours of Hercules on the gables of the temple, omitting the killing of the Stymphelian birds and the cleansing of the country of Elis. A representation of Hercules wrestling with Antaeus appears instead.

l: Thebes, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XI.
s: The Thebans identify the ruins, inscriptions, monuments, statues, and stories described near the Electris gate. They say that the old wooden statue in the temple of Hercules called Champion was made by Daedalus, and that Historis helped Alcmena give birth by deceiving the Sorceresses.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XII.
s: The Thebans are said to have begun sacrificing oxen used for labor to Apollo Spodius after once sacrificing an ox from a nearby waggon. They say that Cadmus was guided to the site of Thebes by a marked cow, founded his home there, and established an altar and statue of Athene Onga. The account describes ruins associated with Cadmus, Harmonia, and Semele, along with traditions concerning Dionysus Cadmus and statues at Thebes. It also commemorates Pronomus, who enabled the same flute to be used for different musical measures.

l: Thebans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XII.
s: The Thebans formerly sacrificed bulls to Apollo Spodius, but after sacrificing an ox employed in labor when the intended sacrificial bull failed to arrive, they continued sacrificing working oxen. They say that Cadmus was guided by a marked cow to the place where he and his army settled, and they erected statues there to Pronomus and Epaminondas.

l: Thebes, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XII.
s: Thebes is identified as the place where Cadmus and his army made their home after the guiding cow lay down. The account places an altar and statue of Athene Onga, the ruins of the bridal chambers of Harmonia and Semele, and statues and an altar associated with Dionysus in the citadel or market-place area.

l: Cadmus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XII.
s: Cadmus was said to have travelled from Delphi toward Phocis with a cow purchased from Pelagon's herds, whose markings resembled full moons. Following an oracle, he settled with his army where the cow lay down, and he is credited with erecting an altar and statue of Athene; Polydorus later adorned a heavenly piece of wood connected with Cadmus and called it Dionysus Cadmus.

l: Pronomus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XII.
s: Pronomus was a highly attractive flute-player who discovered that flutes could be used for every kind of measure and was the first to play different measures on the same flute. His appearance and bodily movements delighted theatre audiences, and a processional song of his remained in use among the people of Chalcis near the Euripus who had come to Delos; the Thebans erected a statue of him.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIII.
s: Epaminondas led the Thebans at Leuctra after the Bœotarchs voted to risk a battle against the Lacedæmonians. The Lacedæmonians, commanded by King Cleombrotus, were defeated after Cleombrotus and many prominent Lacedæmonians fell. The Thebans and their remaining Bœotian forces lost 47 men, while the Lacedæmonians lost more than 1,000.

l: Epaminondas, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIII.
s: Epaminondas was of illustrious descent but grew up in poverty and studied under Lysis the Tarentine, a pupil of Pythagoras. He once risked his life to rescue Pelopidas, challenged the Lacedæmonians during an embassy to Sparta, and led the decision to fight at Leuctra. After the victory, he required the Lacedæmonians’ allies to bury their dead first so that their losses would be revealed.

l: Thebans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIII.
s: The Thebans fought the Lacedæmonians at Leuctra, staking the safety of their country, wives, and children on the battle. They won the engagement, with only 47 Thebans and Bœotians who remained in the battle killed.

l: Lacedæmonians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIII.
s: The Lacedæmonians attacked the Thebans with their own forces and those of their allies. They were defeated at Leuctra, lost more than 1,000 men, and buried their dead only after their allies had done so.

l: Bœotia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIII.
s: Bœotia was the region in which Leuctra lay, and the various towns of Bœotia were discussed during the peace associated with Antalcidas. Bœotian forces fought with the Thebans, though the Thespians and other Bœotians hostile to the Thebans withdrew before the battle.

l: Sparta, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIII.
s: Sparta was the place where Epaminondas served on an embassy when the Lacedæmonians agreed to ratify the peace of Antalcidas. When Agesilaus asked whether the Bœotian towns would subscribe separately, Epaminondas answered that they would not do so until Sparta’s neighboring towns set the example.

l: Cleombrotus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIII.
s: Cleombrotus, king of the Lacedæmonians, turned aside to Ambrosus in Phocis, passed through after killing Chæreas and his men, and reached Leuctra. He fell in the battle against the Thebans.

l: Leuctra, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIII.
s: Leuctra in Bœotia was the site of the battle between the Thebans and the Lacedæmonians. Scedasus had lived there, and Epaminondas offered funeral rites to Scedasus and his daughters and vowed that a battle would take place there.

l: Bœotarchs, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIII.
s: The Bœotarchs disagreed over whether to engage the Lacedæmonians or prepare for a siege. Their votes were initially divided equally, but Bacchylides, the seventh Bœotarch, returned from Cithæron and voted with Epaminondas, leading them to choose battle.

l: allies of the Lacedæmonians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIII.
s: The allies of the Lacedæmonians had previously been dissatisfied with them and showed their hostility during the engagement by giving way wherever the enemy attacked. Some suffered no deaths, while others lost only a few men, unlike the Lacedæmonians.

l: battle of Leuctra, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIII.
s: The battle of Leuctra was a major victory for the Thebans over the Lacedæmonians and was described as the most notable victory won by Greeks over Greeks. Cleombrotus and many high-ranking Lacedæmonians were killed, and the Lacedæmonians lost more than 1,000 men compared with 47 Theban and Bœotian dead.

l: war between the Lacedæmonians and the Thebans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIII.
s: The war began after the Lacedæmonians and the Thebans came into conflict, with the Lacedæmonians attacking the Thebans alongside their allies. The war included the battle at Leuctra, where the Thebans defeated the Lacedæmonians.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIV.
s: After the battle at Leuctra, Epaminondas released the other Peloponnesians but kept the Lacedæmonians shut up until he heard that the Spartans were coming to relieve them. He captured Ceressus, took the Thespians there captive, and then intervened in the Peloponnese by supporting the Argives, restoring Mantinea, and establishing Megalopolis for the Arcadians. Epaminondas continued as Bœotarch beyond the lawful term, marched against Sparta, and began the colonization of Messene while the Theban allies plundered Laconia. He later routed Iphicrates and his Athenians near Lechæum, pursued them toward Athens, returned to Thebes, and was acquitted for remaining in office.

l: Epaminondas, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIV.
s: Epaminondas released the other Peloponnesians after the battle but kept the Lacedæmonians shut up at Leuctra until he heard that the Spartans were coming to relieve them. He captured Ceressus, supported the Arcadians in the Peloponnese, restored Mantinea, established Megalopolis, continued as Bœotarch beyond the lawful term, marched against Sparta, and turned to the colonization of Messene. He later routed Iphicrates and his forces near Lechæum, pursued them toward Athens, and was acquitted for continuing as Bœotarch.

l: Lacedæmonians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIV.
s: The Lacedæmonians were kept shut up at Leuctra by Epaminondas after the battle. When the Spartans came in full force to relieve them, Epaminondas allowed them to depart on conditions of war.

l: Leuctra, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIV.
s: Leuctra was the place where the Lacedæmonians were kept shut up after the battle. An oracle also described shady Leuctra as dear to it and foretold a lamentable battle there.

l: battle of Leuctra, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIV.
s: Directly after the Battle of Leuctra, Epaminondas released the other Peloponnesians and detained the Lacedæmonians at Leuctra. The text connects the battle with the subsequent events involving the Thespians, the Peloponnese, and Sparta.

l: Thespians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIV.
s: The Thespians, regretting their former ill-will toward the Thebans and fearing their current fortunes, abandoned their city and fled to Ceressus. After Epaminondas captured Ceressus, he took the Thespians who had taken refuge there captive.

l: Peloponnese, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIV.
s: Epaminondas turned his attention to the Peloponnese after capturing Ceressus because the Arcadians eagerly invited his cooperation. He made the Argives his voluntary allies, restored Mantinea, and helped establish Megalopolis.

l: Arcadians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIV.
s: The Arcadians invited Epaminondas to cooperate in the Peloponnese. He persuaded them to evacuate their insecure small towns and established one large town for them, called Megalopolis.

l: Mantinea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIV.
s: Epaminondas restored the Mantineans, who had been dispersed into villages by Agesipolis, to Mantinea.

l: Megalopolis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIV.
s: Megalopolis was established by Epaminondas for the Arcadians after he persuaded them to evacuate their insecure small towns. It was one large town and was still called Megalopolis.

l: Bœotarch, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIV.
s: Epaminondas’s period of office as Bœotarch expired, and the law imposed death as the penalty for continuing in office beyond the proper time. He disregarded the law, continued as Bœotarch, and was later acquitted because none of the judges would sentence him.

l: Sparta, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIV.
s: Spartans came in full force to relieve the Lacedæmonians at Leuctra. Epaminondas later marched with an army against Sparta, but Agesilaus declined to fight.

l: Messene, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIV.
s: After Agesilaus declined a combat at Sparta, Epaminondas turned his attention toward colonizing Messene.

l: colonization of Messene, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIV.
s: The colonization of Messene was undertaken by Epaminondas after he marched against Sparta and Agesilaus declined a combat.

l: Theban allies, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIV.
s: The Theban allies overran Laconia and plundered it, scouring the whole country. Their actions induced Epaminondas to take the Thebans back into Bœotia.

l: Laconia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIV.
s: Laconia was overrun and plundered throughout by the Theban allies.

l: Thebans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIV.
s: The Thebans were taken back into Bœotia by Epaminondas after their allies had overrun and plundered Laconia.

l: Bœotia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIV.
s: Epaminondas took the Thebans back into Bœotia after the Theban allies had plundered Laconia. He returned to Thebes after pursuing Iphicrates’s forces toward Athens.

l: Iphicrates, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIV.
s: Iphicrates, the son of Timotheus, attacked Epaminondas near Lechæum with Athenians and some targeteers. Epaminondas routed and pursued his forces as far as Athens, but Iphicrates would not allow the Athenians to go out and fight.

l: Athenians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIV.
s: The Athenians, together with some targeteers, accompanied Iphicrates in attacking Epaminondas near Lechæum. After Epaminondas routed them and pursued them toward Athens, Iphicrates prevented them from going out to fight.

l: Athens, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIV.
s: Epaminondas pursued Iphicrates and the Athenians as far as Athens. He returned to Thebes when Iphicrates would not allow the Athenians to go out and fight.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XV.
s: Alexander, ruler in Thessaly, treacherously imprisoned Pelopidas, prompting the Thebans to march against him. When Epaminondas took command near Pylæ, Alexander lost confidence and released Pelopidas. Epaminondas later defeated Lacedæmonians, Achæans, and Athenians, showed mercy to Bœotian deserters, and was killed by an Athenian at Mantinea. He was praised for restoring Messene, helping Megalopolis, and bringing freedom and autonomy to Greece.

l: Alexander, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XV.
s: Alexander, the ruler in Thessaly, treacherously imprisoned Pelopidas, who had come to his court as a personal and public friend. When Epaminondas took command of the Theban force near Pylæ, Alexander lost confidence in victory and released Pelopidas.

l: Pelopidas, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XV.
s: Pelopidas was imprisoned by Alexander while visiting him as a personal friend and a friend of the Theban people. He was released after Epaminondas took command of the Theban force.

l: Thebans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XV.
s: The Thebans marched against Alexander after he imprisoned Pelopidas, putting Cleomenes and Hypatus at their head. During Epaminondas's absence, they drove the Orchomenians from their country, an act Epaminondas regarded as a misfortune.

l: Epaminondas, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XV.
s: Epaminondas took command of the Theban force near Pylæ, causing Alexander to release Pelopidas. As Bœotarch, he defeated the Lacedæmonians, Achæans, and Athenians, spared Bœotian deserters at Phœbia by stigmatizing them, and was killed by an Athenian at Mantinea in the moment of victory. He was credited with restoring Messene and helping the Greeks gain freedom.

l: Greeks, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XV.
s: The Greeks were said to have gained their freedom through Epaminondas.

l: Sparta, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XV.
s: Sparta was said to have cut off the glory from the councils, before sacred Messene recovered her children.

l: Messene, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XV.
s: Messene was restored by Epaminondas, and her children returned to her.

l: Thebes, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XV.
s: The arms of Thebes crowned Megalopolis.

l: Greece, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XV.
s: Greece became autonomous and free through the deeds associated with Epaminondas.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVI.
s: Near the statue of Epaminondas, Thebes has a temple of Ammon with a statue by Calamis and a hymn by Pindar inscribed nearby. The Thebans also have a temple of Fortune, ancient wooden statues of Aphrodite attributed to Harmonia, and a temple of Law-giving Demeter. At the gate called Prœtis, there are a theatre and the temple of Lysian Dionysus, who freed Thebans captured by Thracians. The area also contains ruins of the house of Lycus, the sepulchre of Semele, and monuments to the children of Amphion.

l: Ammon, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVI.
s: Ammon has a temple near the statue of Epaminondas. His statue there was made by Calamis, and Pindar dedicated a votive offering and a hymn in his honour; the hymn is inscribed on a triangular pillar near the altar dedicated by Ptolemy the son of Lagus.

l: temple of Ammon, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVI.
s: The temple of Ammon stands near the statue of Epaminondas. It contains a statue of Ammon by Calamis, while a hymn by Pindar is inscribed on a triangular pillar near its altar.

l: Thebes, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVI.
s: Thebes has a temple of Ammon, Tiresias’ tower, a temple of Fortune carrying Wealth, ancient wooden statues of Aphrodite, and a temple of Law-giving Demeter. At the gate called Prœtis, it also has a theatre and the temple of Lysian Dionysus, as well as ruins of the house of Lycus, the sepulchre of Semele, and monuments to the children of Amphion.

l: Thebans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVI.
s: The Thebans say that Xenophon the Athenian made the hands and face of the statue of Fortune carrying Wealth, while Callistonicus made the rest. They also say that their ancient wooden statues of Aphrodite were votive offerings of Harmonia and that the shields at the temple of Demeter belonged to Lacedæmonian notables who fell at Leuctra. The Thebans say that Dionysus freed some of their people who had been captured by Thracians.

l: Aphrodite, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVI.
s: The Thebans have three ancient wooden statues of Aphrodite, said to be votive offerings of Harmonia made from the wood of the gunwales of Cadmus’ ships. They call them the Celestial Aphrodite, the Pandemian, and the Heart-Turner, representing pure love, vulgar sensual love, and lawless passion respectively.

l: Harmonia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVI.
s: Harmonia is said to have made the three ancient wooden statues of Aphrodite as votive offerings, using wood from the gunwales of Cadmus’ ships. She associated their titles with pure love, common sensual love, and the turning of men’s hearts toward lawless passion and unholy deeds.

l: Thracians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVI.
s: The Thracians captured some Thebans and conducted them to Haliartia. The captives were freed by Dionysus and given an opportunity to kill the Thracians in their sleep.

l: Dionysus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVI.
s: Dionysus is called Lysian because he freed some Thebans captured by Thracians and enabled them to kill their captors in their sleep. A temple dedicated to Lysian Dionysus stands near the theatre at the gate called Prœtis.

l: temple of Lysian Dionysus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVI.
s: The temple of Lysian Dionysus stands near the theatre at the gate called Prœtis. One of its statues is said by the Thebans to be Semele, and the temple is opened once every year on stated days.

l: Semele, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVI.
s: The temple of Lysian Dionysus contains a statue that the Thebans say is Semele. Her sepulchre is also located there, while the text distinguishes it from the sepulchre of Alcmene because Alcmene became a stone when she died.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVII.
s: The temple of Artemis Euclea contains a statue by Scopas and the burials of Antipœnus’s daughters, who sacrificed themselves so Hercules and the Thebans could defeat the Orchomenians. Near the temple are offerings and statues connected with Hercules, Apollo Boedromius, Hermes Agoræus, and Amphitryon. The sepulchre of Zethus and Amphion is associated with a fertility ritual involving earth carried from Tithorea to Antiope’s tomb. Antiope, driven mad after Dirce’s death, was cured and married by Phocus, and the two were buried together; stones near Amphion’s tomb were said to have followed his music.

l: temple of Artemis Euclea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVII.
s: The temple contains a statue of Artemis Euclea by Scopas and is said to contain the burials of Androclea and Alcis, the daughters of Antipœnus. A stone lion in front of it was reportedly dedicated by Hercules after his victory over the Orchomenians and their king Erginus.

l: Hercules, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVII.
s: Hercules was preparing to fight the Orchomenians with the Thebans when an oracle required the voluntary death of one of the most notable citizens for victory. He dedicated a stone lion before the temple of Artemis Euclea after defeating the Orchomenians and Erginus.

l: Thebans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVII.
s: The Thebans were going to battle against the Orchomenians with Hercules. They believed they would win if a prominent citizen willingly committed suicide, and they later guarded the sepulchre of Zethus and Amphion when people from Tithorea sought to remove its earth.

l: Orchomenians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVII.
s: The Orchomenians fought Hercules and the Thebans and were defeated, along with their king Erginus the son of Clymenus.

l: Amphion, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVII.
s: Amphion is buried with Zethus in a mound of earth. His funeral pile lies about half a stade from his tomb, and stones near the tomb were said to have followed his music.

l: sepulchre of Zethus and Amphion, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVII.
s: The sepulchre is a low mound of earth. The people of Tithorea sought to carry away earth from it when the Sun was in Taurus and place it on Antiope’s tomb, while the Thebans guarded it because they believed this would make Tithorea fertile and cause blight in Thebes.

l: Zethus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVII.
s: Zethus is buried with Amphion in a low mound of earth. His sepulchre was involved in the ritual by which people from Tithorea attempted to improve the fertility of their land.

l: Tithorea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVII.
s: The inhabitants of Tithorea sought to carry earth from the sepulchre of Zethus and Amphion and place it on Antiope’s tomb when the Sun was in Taurus. They believed this would increase the fertility of their land, though the Thebans believed it would cause their own land’s fruits to suffer blight.

l: Antiope, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVII.
s: Antiope was driven mad and wandered through Greece after Dirce’s cruel death, which was attributed to Dionysus’s anger toward her. Phocus cured her and married her, and she was buried with him; her tomb was also the intended destination for earth taken from the sepulchre of Zethus and Amphion.

l: Phocus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVII.
s: Phocus, the son of Ornytion and grandson of Sisyphus, found Antiope while she was wandering in madness. He cured and married her, and he was buried with her.

l: tomb of Amphion, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVII.
s: Amphion’s tomb is near his funeral pile. Stones lying near it in no particular order were said to be the stones that followed Amphion’s music.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: The road from Thebes to Chalcis passes the tomb of Melanippus, three stones said to mark Tydeus’s burial, and the tombs of the children of Œdipus. The Thebans perform funeral sacrifices for several heroes and for the children of Œdipus, during which the flame and smoke are said to divide. They show a cenotaph of Tiresias and the tomb of Hector near the Well of Œdipus, claiming Hector’s remains were brought from Ilium in response to an oracle. The Well of Œdipus is said to be where Œdipus washed away the blood from his father’s murder.

l: Thebes, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: Thebes is connected by a high road to Chalcis through the gate Prœtis. The Thebans identify several tombs and sites along the road, perform funeral sacrifices for heroes and the children of Œdipus, and claim that Hector’s remains were brought from Ilium to their city.

l: Melanippus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: Melanippus is described as one of the greatest warriors of the Thebans. During the Argive siege of Thebes, he slew Tydeus and Mecisteus, and Amphiaraus is said to have slain him.

l: Tydeus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: Tydeus was slain by Melanippus during the Argive siege of Thebes. Three rude stones near Melanippus’s tomb are said by Theban antiquarians to mark Tydeus’s burial, and Mæon is said to have buried him.

l: sons of Œdipus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: The children of Œdipus have tombs near the road from Thebes to Chalcis. The Thebans offer funeral sacrifices to them, during which the flame and smoke are said to divide.

l: Œdipus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: The Well of Œdipus is named because Œdipus washed away in it the blood from the murder of his father.

l: Tiresias, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: The Thebans show a tomb of Tiresias about 15 stades from the tombs of the children of Œdipus. They admit that Tiresias died in Haliartia, so they regard the tomb as a cenotaph.

l: Hector, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: Hector, the son of Priam, is said to have a tomb near the Well of Œdipus. The Thebans claim that his remains were brought from Ilium to Thebes in accordance with an oracle promising their city abundant wealth if they honored him.

l: Well of Œdipus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: The Well of Œdipus is near the tomb of Hector and is named for Œdipus’s washing away there the blood from his father’s murder.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIX.
s: Teumessus is associated with the hiding of Europa by Zeus, the Teumessian fox, and a temple of Athene Telchinia. The area around Glisas contains tombs, mythic landmarks, and ruins of Harma and Mycalessus, while Mycalessus has a temple of Mycalessian Demeter whose statue receives fruits that remain fresh. At Aulis, near the Euripus, a temple of Artemis commemorates the substitution of a doe for Iphigenia and preserves the remains of a plane-tree mentioned by Homer. The Greeks sacrificed various victims to Artemis after favorable winds appeared, and Aulis is inhabited mainly by potters.

l: Teumessus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIX.
s: Teumessus is the place where Europa was said to have been hidden by Zeus. Its fox was brought up to harm the Thebans through the wrath of Dionysus, but it and the dog that was about to catch it were turned into stone. Teumessus also has a temple of Athene Telchinia without a statue.

l: Artemis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIX.
s: Artemis gave Procris, the daughter of Erechtheus, a dog that pursued the fox of Teumessus until both animals were turned into stone. At Aulis, she caused a doe to be sacrificed instead of Iphigenia, and the Greeks later sacrificed various victims to her when favorable winds appeared.

l: Bœotia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIX.
s: Bœotia is the region in which Teumessus, Glisas, Harma, Mycalessus, and Aulis are situated. The Telchinians formerly dwelt at Cyprus and migrated into Bœotia, where some of them were said to have erected the temple of Athene Telchinia.

l: Glisas, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIX.
s: Glisas is represented by ruins located about seven stades beyond Teumessus. Above it is a mountain called Highest, which bears the temple and altar of Highest Zeus, and the torrent there is called Thermodon.

l: Mycalessus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIX.
s: Mycalessus was said to have received its name because the cow leading Cadmus and his army to Thebes lowed there. It was previously described as having been depopulated, and near the sea it has a temple of Mycalessian Demeter.

l: Mycalessian Demeter, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIX.
s: Mycalessian Demeter has a temple near the sea at Mycalessus. Fruits of Autumn placed at the feet of her statue remain fresh throughout the year.

l: temple of Mycalessian Demeter, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIX.
s: The temple of Mycalessian Demeter near the sea is said to be shut and opened every night by Hercules, who is identified as one of the Idæan Dactyli. Fruits of Autumn placed before the statue inside it remain fresh all year.

l: Aulis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIX.
s: Aulis lies near the place where the Euripus separates Eubœa from Bœotia and is said to have been named after the daughter of Ogygus. It contains a temple of Artemis, the remains of the plane-tree mentioned by Homer, a well, a brazen threshold associated with Agamemnon's tent, and palm trees. Aulis has few inhabitants, who are potters, and its district is inhabited by the people of Tanagra.

l: temple of Artemis at Aulis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIX.
s: The temple of Artemis at Aulis contains two stone statues of Artemis, one holding torches and the other resembling an archer. It is associated with the sacrifice of a doe in place of Iphigenia, the remains of the plane-tree mentioned by Homer, and a custom of accepting all kinds of victims.

l: Greeks, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIX.
s: The Greeks at Aulis were preparing to sacrifice Iphigenia in accordance with the oracle of Calchas when Artemis caused a doe to be sacrificed instead. Their wind was initially unfavorable, but after a favorable wind appeared they sacrificed to Artemis whatever male and female victims they had.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XX.
s: Delium is a place near the sea in the district of Tanagra with statues of Artemis and Leto. The people of Tanagra trace their founder, Pœmander, through a genealogy connected to Apollo and say that Tanagra was his wife, though Corinna gives her a different parentage. Tanagra was also called Graia for a long time because Tanagra lived to an advanced age, but it later regained the name Tanagra. At Tanagra, traditions describe Orion's tomb, Hermes's upbringing, Atlas's meditation, and two accounts of Triton's defeat and death.

l: Delium, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XX.
s: Delium is a place in the part of the district of Tanagra near the sea. It contains statues of Artemis and Leto.

l: people of Tanagra, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XX.
s: The people of Tanagra say that Pœmander was their founder and that Tanagra was his wife. They also say that people living nearby called Tanagra Graia because she lived to a very advanced age, and that the city was eventually called Graia before regaining the name Tanagra.

l: Pœmander, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XX.
s: Pœmander is identified as the founder of Tanagra. He was the son of Chæresilaus, the son of Iasius, the son of Eleuther, who was the son of Apollo by Æthusa, the daughter of Poseidon; Pœmander married Tanagra.

l: Tanagra, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XX.
s: Tanagra was said by the people of Tanagra to be the daughter of Æolus and the wife of Pœmander, while Corinna said she was the daughter of Asopus. Because she lived to a very advanced age, she was called Graia, and the city later bore that name before recovering the name Tanagra.

l: Graia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XX.
s: Graia was the name given to Tanagra because of her exceptionally long life, and the city was also called Graia for a long period. Homer used Graia as the city's name in his Catalogue.

l: temple of Dionysus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XX.
s: The temple of Dionysus at Tanagra contains a statue of Dionysus by Calamis in Parian stone. It also contains a statue of Triton that is described as even more wonderful.

l: Dionysus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XX.
s: Dionysus was prayed to by the women of Tanagra when Triton attacked them during their bathing in the sea, and he came to their aid and defeated Triton. In another account, Triton was thought to have been killed by Dionysus because he was captured while drunk.

l: Triton at Tanagra, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XX.
s: Triton is represented by a notable statue at the temple of Dionysus. One tradition says he attacked the women of Tanagra and was defeated by Dionysus; another says he ambushed herds, plundered small vessels, drank wine given to him, fell asleep, and was killed after a man of Tanagra struck off his head with an axe.

l: statue of Triton, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XX.
s: The statue of Triton at the temple of Dionysus is considered especially wonderful. It has no head because, according to one legend, a man of Tanagra struck Triton's head off with an axe.

l: women of Tanagra, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XX.
s: Before the orgies of Dionysus, the women of Tanagra bathed in the sea to purify themselves. Triton attacked them while they were swimming, and they prayed to Dionysus for help.

l: orgies of Dionysus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XX.
s: Before the orgies of Dionysus, the women of Tanagra bathed in the sea to purify themselves.

l: women's bathing in the sea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XX.
s: The women of Tanagra bathed in the sea before the orgies of Dionysus in order to purify themselves.

l: Triton's assault on the women, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XX.
s: Triton assaulted the women of Tanagra while they were swimming in the sea after bathing to purify themselves. They prayed to Dionysus for aid.

l: fight between Dionysus and Triton, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XX.
s: According to an ancient legend, Dionysus answered the women's prayer and fought Triton. Dionysus conquered Triton.

l: Triton's ambush of the herds, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XX.
s: According to a more plausible but less ancient legend, Triton lay in ambush when herds were driven to the sea and carried some of them off. He also plundered small vessels.

l: killing of Triton, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XX.
s: In one account, the people of Tanagra filled a bowl with wine for Triton, and he drank it, fell asleep, and tumbled down the rocks. A man of Tanagra then struck off his head with an axe; because Triton was captured while drunk, they thought he was killed by Dionysus.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXI.
s: The speaker describes the appearance of Tritons and several unusual animals, including Ethiopian bulls, Indian camels, the elk, and the tiger. Ethiopian bulls are called rhinoceroses because of their nose horns, while the elk is a difficult-to-hunt animal found among the Celts. The speaker identifies the Indian manslayer, or martiora, as a tiger but rejects the Indian claims that it has three rows of teeth and a projectile tail-sting. The speaker also argues that animals vary by climate and land, citing examples from Greece, Libya, India, Arabia, Ethiopia, and Phrygia.

l: Tritons, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXI.
s: Tritons are described as having frog-wort-like hair, shark-like scales, fish gills under their ears, a human-like nose, a large mouth, animal teeth, greyish-blue eyes, shellfish-like hands and nails, and dolphin-like fins under the breast and belly. The speaker has seen Tritons among the curiosities at Rome and at Tanagra, with the one at Rome being smaller.

l: Ethiopian bulls, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXI.
s: Ethiopian bulls have a horn projecting from the nose and a smaller horn beneath it, but no horns on the head. They are called rhinoceroses because of these nose horns.

l: rhinoceroses, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXI.
s: The name rhinoceroses is applied to the Ethiopian bulls because they have a horn projecting from the nose and another smaller horn beneath it, while lacking horns on the head.

l: India, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXI.
s: India is said to have camels colored like leopards and the wild animal called the martiora by its inhabitants and the manslayer by the Greeks. The speaker also says that remote India may contain wild animals unlike those found in Greece.

l: elk, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXI.
s: The elk is a wild animal found among the Celts and described as something between a stag and a camel. It is difficult to hunt or see at a distance because it scents humans from far away and hides among rocks and caves; hunters usually capture it only when it is enclosed accidentally within a large net.

l: tiger, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXI.
s: The speaker identifies the Indian martiora, or manslayer described by Ctesias, as a tiger. The speaker rejects the reports that the tiger has three rows of teeth in each jaw and a tail that stings and shoots its stings like arrows, and explains its apparently uniform red color as an effect of sunlight, speed, or constant motion.

l: Indians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXI.
s: Indians are said to report that the tiger has three rows of teeth in each jaw and a tail with stings that it can hurl at a distance. The speaker believes they accept this account because of their excessive terror of the animal and says they are also mistaken about its color.

l: wild animals, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXI.
s: Wild animals differ between climates and lands, so animals found in remote Libya, India, or Arabia would not necessarily be the same as those found in Greece. Their appearance and kinds are presented as subject to the conditions of different regions.

l: Greece, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXI.
s: Greece is used as the standard for comparison with the remote regions of Libya, India, and Arabia. The speaker says that someone seeking the wild animals found in Greece would not find them in those distant lands, but would encounter different animals.

l: Libya, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXI.
s: Libya is named as a region whose remote parts may contain wild animals unlike those found in Greece. Its asps are said to have the same color as the Egyptian asps.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXII.
s: Tanagra is described as having temples to several gods, including Hermes, and as honoring its gods by keeping houses and temples separate in pure places. Its traditions include Hermes carrying a ram to end a pestilence, Corinna’s victory over Pindar, and distinctive kinds of cocks. In Boeotia, Anthedon lies at the foot of Mount Messapium on the sea and contains temples, tombs, and a place associated with Glaucus. Glaucus was a fisherman who became a marine god after eating a certain grass and was believed to predict the future.

l: Tanagra, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXII.
s: Tanagra has temples to Dionysus, Themis, Aphrodite, Apollo, Artemis, Leto, and Hermes. Its people keep their houses and temples apart, place the temples in pure locations, honor their gods greatly, and preserve traditions about Hermes, Corinna, and two kinds of cocks.

l: Bœotia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXII.
s: Boeotia has Mount Messapium on the left of the Euripus, with Anthedon at its foot on the sea.

l: Apollo, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXII.
s: Apollo has a temple at Tanagra near temples of Artemis and Leto. He is said to have slain Otus and Ephialtes, as represented by Homer and Pindar.

l: Hermes, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXII.
s: Hermes is worshipped at Tanagra as the Ram-carrier and the Champion. He is said to have ended a pestilence by carrying a ram around the walls, and Calamis made a statue of him carrying a ram; he is also said to have led Tanagra’s young men against the Eretrians and helped rout them with a scraper. Purslane is preserved in his temple as the Champion because it was believed that he was reared under that tree.

l: Corinna, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXII.
s: Corinna is described as the only poetess of Tanagra. She has a tomb in a conspicuous place in the town and a painting in the gymnasium, showing her with a fillet because of her victory over Pindar at Thebes; the text attributes her victory partly to her Aeolic dialect and her beauty.

l: Pindar, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXII.
s: Pindar was defeated by Corinna at Thebes. The text suggests that Corinna’s use of Aeolic, rather than the Doric used by Pindar, helped her win.

l: Anthedon, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXII.
s: Anthedon is a Boeotian city on the sea at the foot of Mount Messapium. It has a grove and temple of the Cabiri, temples of Demeter and Proserpine and of Dionysus, the tombs of Otus and Ephialtes, and the place called the leap of Glaucus.

l: Glaucus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXII.
s: Glaucus was a fisherman who became a marine god after eating a certain grass. He is believed, especially by seafaring men, to predict the future, and Pindar and Aeschylus celebrated him, with Aeschylus making him the subject of one of his plays.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: The Thebans have the gymnasium of Iolaus, a race-course, and the hero-chapel of Iolaus near the gate Prœtis, while the Hippodrome contains the tomb of Pindar. Pindar was said to have begun writing poetry after bees made honey on his lips as he slept, and he later received honors connected with Apollo and Proserpine. Acræphnium, situated on Mount Ptoum, contains a notable temple and statue of Dionysus, while the nearby temple of Ptoan Apollo once housed an infallible oracle. Beyond Mount Ptoum lies Larymna, a Boeotian coastal city with a temple and statue of Dionysus, a deep harbor, and mountains suitable for wild-boar hunting.

l: Thebans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: The Thebans have the gymnasium of Iolaus, a race-course, and the hero-chapel of Iolaus near the gate Prœtis. They admit that Iolaus died in Sardinia with the Athenians and Thespians who crossed over with him. Some Thebans who escaped the destruction of Thebes by Alexander fled to Acræphnium because old age and weakness prevented them from reaching Attica.

l: tomb of Pindar, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: The tomb of Pindar is situated in the Hippodrome near the race-course of Iolaus.

l: Pindar, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: Pindar began writing poems after bees settled on him while he slept and made honey on his lips. When he became famous throughout Greece, the Pythian Priestess proclaimed at Delphi that he should receive an equal share of the firstfruits with Apollo. In old age he dreamed that Proserpine told him he had not celebrated her, and he died before the tenth day after the dream; afterward, a woman related to him dreamed that he recited a Hymn to Proserpine and wrote it down when she awoke.

l: Thebes, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: Thebes was destroyed by Alexander, and some of its inhabitants fled to Acræphnium. Before the invasion of Alexander and the Macedonians and the destruction of Thebes, the oracle of Ptoan Apollo was regarded as infallible.

l: Acræphnium, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: Acræphnium was originally said to have been a city in the district of Thebes. It is situated on Mount Ptoum and contains a temple and statue of Dionysus that are described as worth seeing.

l: Ptoan Apollo, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: Ptoan Apollo was worshipped at a temple about fifteen stades from Acræphnium. The god's name was connected with Ptous, the son of Athamas and Themisto, according to the poet Asius.

l: temple of Ptoan Apollo, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: The temple of Ptoan Apollo stood about fifteen stades beyond Acræphnium on Mount Ptoum. Before Alexander's invasion and the destruction of Thebes, it was associated with an infallible oracle.

l: oracle of Ptoan Apollo, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: The oracle of Ptoan Apollo was once considered infallible. When Mys, a European sent by Mardonius, consulted it in his own language, the god answered not in Greek but in the Carian dialect.

l: Larymna, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: Larymna is a Boeotian coastal city named after Larymna, the daughter of Cynus. It was formerly reckoned with Opus, but when the Thebans became powerful its inhabitants voluntarily transferred themselves to the Boeotians. The city has a temple and standing statue of Dionysus, a deep harbor, and mountains above it that provide good wild-boar hunting.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: The text describes the area around Lake Cephisis, also called Copais, and the settlements along its shores. The river Cephisus rises at Lilæa in Phocis and flows into the lake. Several former towns near the lake were reportedly destroyed by a winter flood, while the lake is known for its fish, especially its eels. The account then follows the route through nearby villages and towns to the river Platanius, which flows into the sea near Halæ.

l: lake Cephisis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: Lake Cephisis, also called Copais by some, receives the river Cephisus. Several small towns formerly stood near it, including Athenæ and Eleusis, but the Bœotians say that a winter flood swept them away. Its fish resemble those of other lakes, while its eels are especially fine and good to eat.

l: Cephisus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: The river Cephisus rises at Lilæa in Phocis and has its outlet into Lake Cephisis.

l: river Platanius, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: The river Platanius has its outlet into the sea below Corsea. The town of Halæ lies on its right near the sea, where the Bœotians border Locris and Eubœa.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXV.
s: The unit describes tombs, monuments, temples, and other sacred places in and around Thebes. Menœceus voluntarily killed himself in accordance with an oracle when Polynices and his army came from Argos, while Polynices and Eteocles are said to have killed one another in single combat, and Antigone dragged Polynices’s corpse to Eteocles’s funeral pile. It also recounts traditions about Pindar’s house, local temples, and Hercules. Most of the concluding account concerns the Cabiri, the Cabirian mysteries, their restoration by Pelarge and Isthmiades, and the violent punishments inflicted on those who profaned the temple of the Cabiri.

l: Thebes, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXV.
s: Thebes contains the tomb of Menœceus near the gate Neistis, a monument marking the single combat of the sons of Œdipus, temples to several deities, and places associated with Antigone and Hercules. The Thebans say that the vine first grew at Thebes, though they have no proof, and they preserve traditions about the Cabiri and their mysteries.

l: Menoeceus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXV.
s: Menœceus, the son of Creon, has a tomb near the gate Neistis at Thebes. He voluntarily killed himself in accordance with an oracle from Delphi when Polynices and his army came from Argos.

l: Polynices, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXV.
s: Polynices came from Argos with an army. He and Eteocles are said to have met in single combat and killed one another, and Antigone dragged his corpse to the funeral pile of Eteocles.

l: Antigone, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXV.
s: Antigone could not easily lift Polynices’s corpse, so she dragged it until she could throw it onto the funeral pile of Eteocles. The place where she did this is called Antigone’s Dragging-ground.

l: Demeter, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXV.
s: Cabirian Demeter is associated with a grove near Thebes and with the mysteries of the Cabiri. According to Theban tradition, she became acquainted with Prometheus, one of the Cabiri, and his son Ætnæus, and placed an undisclosed deposit into their hands.

l: grove of Cabirian Demeter and Proserpine, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXV.
s: The grove of Cabirian Demeter and Proserpine lies about twenty-five stades from the road by the gate Neistis. No one may enter it except those who have been initiated.

l: Cabiri, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXV.
s: The Cabiri were said to have been the inhabitants of a former town at the site of the Cabirian sanctuary. The Argives drove them out after the Epigoni captured Thebes, but Telondes and the other Cabiri who had left Cabiræa later returned when the mysteries were reestablished.

l: temple of the Cabiri, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXV.
s: The temple of the Cabiri stood about seven stades from the grove and was considered exceptionally holy. Those who entered it with hostile or profane intent were destroyed: some of Xerxes’ army went mad and perished, and Macedonians who entered during Alexander’s attack on Thebes were killed by lightning and thunderbolts.

l: Cabirian mysteries, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXV.
s: The text declines to disclose the rites of the Cabirian mysteries or the nature of the deposit associated with their origin. The mysteries were a gift of Demeter to the Cabiri, ceased for a time after the Argives expelled them, and were later restored by Pelarge and Isthmiades.

l: Pelarge, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXV.
s: Pelarge, the daughter of Potneus, and her husband Isthmiades reestablished the Cabirian mysteries after they had ceased to be celebrated. She celebrated them beyond the ancient boundaries, and, following an oracle from Dodona, received various honours and was assigned a pregnant victim for sacrifice.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: The text describes the plain of Tenerus, the temple to Hercules surnamed Hippodetes, and the mountain associated with the Sphinx near the temple of the Cabiri. It recounts differing traditions about the Sphinx, including her riddles, piracy, ancestry, and death at the hands of Œdipus. It then describes the ruins of Onchestus and the town of Thespia, including its temples, statues, and a story about a dragon slain through the sacrifice of Cleostratus. Thespia also contains statues of Dionysus, Fortune, Hygiea, Athene the Worker, and Plutus.

l: temple of the Cabiri, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: The temple of the Cabiri serves as a reference point for the plain of Tenerus, the mountain associated with the Sphinx, the ruins of Onchestus, and the route to Thespia.

l: plain of Tenerus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVI.
