s: The plain of Tenerus lies to the right of the temple of the Cabiri. It is named after Tenerus the seer, whom the people consider the son of Apollo and Melia.

l: temple to Hercules surnamed Hippodetes, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: A large temple to Hercules surnamed Hippodetes stands on the plain of Tenerus. It commemorates the story that Hercules took the Orchomenians' horses by night and tied them to their chariots.

l: Hercules, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: Hercules Hippodetes is said to have taken the horses of the Orchomenians by night and tied them to their chariots, giving him the surname Hippodetes.

l: mountain of the Sphinx, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: The mountain of the Sphinx lies a little beyond the temple to Hercules Hippodetes. The Sphinx is said to have used it as her headquarters or as a base for her robberies.

l: Sphinx, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: The Sphinx is said to have recited a riddle that caused the ruin of those she captured. Another tradition makes her a pirate who sailed with a naval force, used Anthedon as her port, and occupied the mountain for robberies. She is also called the illegitimate daughter of Laius, and Œdipus is said to have killed her after defeating her with a superior force from Corinth.

l: riddle of the Sphinx, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: The riddle of the Sphinx was recited to those she captured and brought about their ruin.

l: Œdipus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: Œdipus is said to have slain the Sphinx after defeating her with a superior force brought from Corinth. He learned the oracle given to Cadmus in a dream.

l: Laius, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: Laius is said to have been the father of the Sphinx and to have told her the oracle given to Cadmus. He had sons by mistresses, while the oracle at Delphi referred only to his wife Epicaste and the male children born to her.

l: oracle given to Cadmus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: The oracle given to Cadmus at Delphi was known only to the kings of Thebes. The Sphinx used knowledge of it to test her brothers, claiming that true sons of Laius would know the oracle.

l: Cadmus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: Cadmus received the oracle at Delphi that was later used by the Sphinx to test those claiming royal descent.

l: Onchestus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: Onchestus is described as the son of Poseidon and as the inhabitant of the place whose ruins stand about 15 stades from the mountain of the Sphinx. In the time of the narrator, a statue of Onchestian Poseidon and the grove mentioned by Homer remained there.

l: Thespia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: Thespia lies under Mount Helicon, about 50 stades from the temple of the Cabiri by the leftward route. It is said to have been named after Thespia, the daughter of Asopus, or after Thespius, the son of Erechtheus from Athens. The town contains statues of Zeus Soter, Dionysus, Fortune, Hygiea, Athene the Worker, and Plutus.

l: statue of Zeus Soter, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: Thespia has a brazen statue of Zeus Soter. The statue is associated with the story of the dragon that once infested the town and with the rescue attributed to Zeus.

l: Zeus Soter, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: Zeus Soter is said to have ordered that one of the lads chosen by lot each year be given to the dragon that infested Thespia. He received the title Saviour in connection with the death of the dragon.

l: dragon of Thespia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: The dragon of Thespia once infested the town and was given one youth chosen by lot each year. It was killed when Cleostratus, wearing a specially made breastplate, gave himself to it.

l: Cleostratus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: Cleostratus was the last victim chosen for the dragon of Thespia. He willingly gave himself to the dragon while wearing the breastplate made by Menestratus, knowing that he would die but also kill the monster.

l: Menestratus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: Menestratus was the lover of Cleostratus. He devised a contrivance by making Cleostratus a brazen breastplate whose plates had inward-bent hooks, enabling Cleostratus to kill the dragon.

l: brazen breastplate with hooks, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: The brazen breastplate with hooks was made by Menestratus for Cleostratus. Its plates had inward-bent hooks, allowing Cleostratus to kill the dragon even though he would perish.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVII.
s: The Thespians especially honor Eros, whose worship, traditions, and statues are described, including works by Lysippus, Praxiteles, and Menodorus. The statue by Praxiteles was removed to Rome and later destroyed by fire, while Menodorus's imitation stood at Thespia. Thespia also contains temples and monuments dedicated to Aphrodite, Hercules, the Muses, and others. The account discusses differing traditions about Eros's parentage and Hercules's relations with the daughters of Thestius, as well as the possibility that the temple of Hercules was founded for an older Hercules.

l: Thespians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVII.
s: The Thespians have always honored Eros above the other gods and possess an old rude stone statue of him. They also have a statue of Eros by Menodorus, a temple of Black Aphrodite, a theatre, a marketplace, a statue of Hesiod, a Victory, and a small temple of the Muses.
